title: Sorting Algorithms
relevance: Sorting is a foundational OA/interview topic because it enables faster searching and many algorithms, and interviewers probe stability, complexity bounds, STL choices, and when to use non-comparison sorts or QuickSelect.

phases.goal: Establish what sorting is and the core definitions interviewers expect: in-place, comparison vs non-comparison, stability, and the comparison-sort lower bound.

must_hit.point: A sorting algorithm is in-place if it needs O(1) auxiliary space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states in-place means constant extra space beyond the input array, phrased as O(1) auxiliary space.

must_hit.point: Comparison sorts have a theoretical worst-case lower bound of Ω(n log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the Ω(n log n) floor for sorts that only compare pairs of elements.

must_hit.point: A sort is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements from the original array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains that when two items share a value, the earlier original one stays earlier after sorting.

must_hit.point: Non-comparison sorts can beat the comparison lower bound by exploiting data structure (e.g., integers in a small range).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts comparison sorts with non-comparison approaches that use value/range structure instead of pairwise compares.

probes: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable, and what is the worst-case lower bound for comparison sorts?

hints.1: Think about equal keys and about sorts that only compare pairs of elements.
hints.2: Stability preserves original relative order of ties; comparison sorts cannot beat a well-known asymptotic floor.
hints.3: Stable = equal elements keep input order; comparison sorts are Ω(n log n) worst case; non-comparison can bypass that when the data has usable structure.

phases.goal: Check that the candidate can walk the classical algorithms’ steps: Selection/Bubble/Insertion, Merge/Quick, Counting/Radix, and QuickSelect’s one-sided recursion.

must_hit.point: Selection Sort repeatedly finds the minimum in the unsorted suffix and swaps it with the first unsorted index, growing a sorted prefix.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes scanning for minIdx then swapping into position i each pass.

must_hit.point: Bubble Sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs so the largest remaining value bubbles to the end; an early exit is allowed if a pass makes zero swaps.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions adjacent compares/swaps, end-of-pass placement of the max, and the swapped-flag early stop.

must_hit.point: Insertion Sort takes the next key and shifts larger sorted-prefix elements right until the key’s slot opens.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes storing key, while-shifting greater left elements, then writing key into the hole.

must_hit.point: Merge Sort divides to size-1 subarrays then merges two sorted halves by always taking the smaller front element; its recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), which is O(n log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states divide/conquer/merge and cites the recurrence resolving to O(n log n) in all cases.

must_hit.point: Quick Sort partitions around a pivot so smaller elements are before it and greater-or-equal after, then recurses on both sides.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes pivot choice, two-pointer partition, placing the pivot, then recursing left and right.

must_hit.point: Counting Sort counts frequencies, builds prefix sums for placement indices, then fills the output by iterating the input backward for stability.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sequences count → prefix sums → backward placement into output.

must_hit.point: Radix Sort stably sorts digit by digit from LSD to MSD using Counting Sort as the subroutine (decimal digit base 10 in the notes).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says LSD→MSD passes with a stable counting sort on each digit.

must_hit.point: QuickSelect uses the same partition idea as Quick Sort but only recurses into the side that still contains the k-th index.
must_hit.evidence_hint: After partition, compare k to pIndex and recurse only left or only right (or return if equal).

probes: Walk through how Merge Sort merges two halves, then contrast that with how Quick Sort’s partition places a pivot.
How does Counting Sort place elements so the sort stays stable?

hints.1: For Merge, think pick-smaller-from-fronts; for Quick, think pivot resting place.
hints.2: Merge always splits evenly and merges linearly; Quick rearranges around a pivot then sorts both partitions. Counting uses prefix sums and a backward scan.
hints.3: Merge: temp merge with <= from left for ties, O(n log n) from T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n). Quick: partition then recurse both sides. Counting: frequencies, prefix sums, place from the end of the array.

phases.goal: Lock in time/space/stability tradeoffs across the classical sorts and when non-comparison or partial selection beats a full comparison sort.

must_hit.point: Selection Sort is O(n²) in all cases, O(1) space, and not stable because long-distance swaps can reorder equals.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives all-case quadratic time, in-place O(1), and instability from distant swaps.

must_hit.point: Optimized Bubble Sort and Insertion Sort are O(n²) worst/average but O(n) best case, O(1) space, and stable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties best-case O(n) to early exit / nearly sorted input, and adjacent-only moves for stability.

must_hit.point: Merge Sort is O(n log n) in all cases and stable, but uses O(n) auxiliary space for the temp merge buffer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts guaranteed O(n log n) and stability with linear extra memory.

must_hit.point: Quick Sort averages O(n log n) with O(log n) stack space on average, but worst case is O(n²) time and up to O(n) stack; it is not stable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states average vs worst asymptotics, average O(log n) recursion depth, and instability of partition swaps.

must_hit.point: Counting Sort is O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space (k = max value) and is preferable when k is about the same order as n; Radix is O(d · (n + b)).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites O(n+k) / O(n+k) for counting and O(d·(n+b)) for radix with base b.

must_hit.point: Recursive Bubble/Insertion need O(n) call-stack space versus O(1) for their iterative forms, while remaining stable with the same time bounds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate attributes the extra O(n) specifically to recursion depth.

probes: Compare Merge Sort and Quick Sort on worst-case time, extra space, and stability.
When would you prefer Counting Sort over a comparison sort?

hints.1: List time, auxiliary space, and whether equals keep order for each algorithm.
hints.2: Merge guarantees O(n log n) but pays O(n) memory; Quick is faster on average but can degrade and is unstable; Counting wins when the value range k is small.
hints.3: Merge: always O(n log n), O(n) temp, stable. Quick: avg O(n log n)/O(log n) stack, worst O(n²)/O(n), not stable. Counting: O(n+k) when k≈n beats O(n log n).

phases.goal: Apply sorting knowledge to STL choices, multi-key stability, bounded-integer hints, Top-K via QuickSelect, and data too large for RAM.

must_hit.point: C++ std::sort is typically Introsort (not stable); std::stable_sort is typically Merge Sort.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names Introsort for std::sort and Merge Sort for std::stable_sort.

must_hit.point: Stability matters for multi-key sorts (e.g., sort by primary key then secondary key) so earlier equal primary keys keep secondary order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains chaining sorts or stable secondary-then-primary style reasoning.

must_hit.point: If elements are bounded in a small integer range (interview example: between 1 and 1000), prefer Counting Sort over a general comparison sort.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate reaches for counting when the interviewer caps the value domain.

must_hit.point: For the k-th element, QuickSelect (or std::nth_element) gives expected O(n) time versus full sort O(n log n) or a priority queue O(n log k).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate chooses QuickSelect/nth_element and contrasts those three asymptotics.

must_hit.point: If data does not fit in RAM, use External Merge Sort: sort RAM-sized chunks to disk, then merge the chunks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes chunking, sorting each chunk, writing back, and merging from disk.

must_hit.point: Introsort mixes Quick Sort with a Heap Sort fallback specifically to avoid O(n²) TLE from bad Quick Sort pivots.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate links Introsort’s heap fallback to guarding against quadratic Quick Sort.

probes: You only need the k-th smallest element—why not fully sort?
std::sort vs std::stable_sort—what’s the practical difference, and when does Counting Sort get hinted?

hints.1: Think partial selection, STL stability, and bounded integer ranges.
hints.2: QuickSelect discards one partition side each step; std::sort is Introsort/unstable while stable_sort is Merge; tiny value domains scream counting.
hints.3: Use QuickSelect/nth_element for expected O(n); std::sort≈Introsort (not stable), std::stable_sort≈Merge; bounds like 1..1000 → Counting Sort; huge-on-disk data → External Merge Sort.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Merge Sort is O(n log n) in all cases, stable, and needs O(n) auxiliary space. Quick Sort averages O(n log n) with about O(log n) stack space and is in-place on the array, but can hit O(n²) time and O(n) stack on bad pivots and is not stable.

Comparison sorts are stuck at Ω(n log n) worst case. Counting Sort is O(n + k) time and space and beats O(n log n) when k≈n; Radix Sort extends that to larger integers at O(d · (n + b)) using stable digit passes.

tradeoffs.topic: Full sort vs QuickSelect for the k-th element
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A full sort costs O(n log n); a heap-based Top-K is O(n log k). QuickSelect only recurses into the needed partition side and has expected O(n) average time (worst O(n²) on bad pivots); C++ exposes this pattern as std::nth_element.
Same asymptotic time and stability, but recursive versions use O(n) call-stack space while iterative versions stay O(1) auxiliary space.
std::sort is typically Introsort and not stable; std::stable_sort is typically Merge Sort and preserves equal-element order when stability is required.

gotchas.trap: Always picking the first element as Quick Sort’s pivot on an already sorted or reverse-sorted array.
gotchas.correction: Partitions become size 0 and size n-1, degenerating to O(n²). Use a randomized pivot or median-of-three to avoid TLE.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Selection Sort is stable because it only moves the minimum into place.
gotchas.correction: It is not stable: the long-distance swap can jump over and reorder equal elements.

gotchas.trap: Implementing Merge Sort’s merge with a strict < when comparing the two halves.
gotchas.correction: Use <= so equal elements from the left half are taken first, which keeps Merge Sort stable.

gotchas.trap: Building Counting Sort’s output by scanning the input forward.
gotchas.correction: Iterate backward during placement so equal keys keep original relative order and the sort stays stable.

gotchas.trap: Fully sorting (or using a heap) when only the k-th element is required.
gotchas.correction: QuickSelect finds the k-th element in expected O(n) time by discarding the irrelevant partition side; std::nth_element follows the same idea.

gotchas.trap: Reaching for a comparison sort when the interviewer bounds values tightly (e.g., between 1 and 1000).
gotchas.correction: That hint points to Counting Sort (or similar non-comparison), which can run in linear time in n+k for small k.
